newsitem.title: GERMANY: IFO forecasts German growth of 2.5 pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: IFO forecasts German growth of 2.5 pct in 1997.

text.p: Germany's highly-regarded IFO economic institute on Monday predicted that German economic growth would accelerate to 2.5 percent in 1997, but said jobless levels would remain high.

IFO analysts told a news conference that jobless levels would remain at an average of 4.1 million in 1997, representing a rate of 10.7 percent, and that Germany's hopes of halving joblessness by the year 2000 could not be realised.
With little improvement expected on the jobs front, the pace of Germany's economic recovery next year would likely lag behind previous recovery phases, the institute predicted.
IFO predicted a real growth in German gross domestic product of 2.5 percent in 1997 and said consumer price inflation would remain moderate at 1.5 percent.
The institute said it expected an improvement in Germany's deficits next year because of further efforts at consolidation and additional revenues due to the economic upswing.
Germany's budget deficit should fall by around 18 billion marks to 118 billion marks, sending its 1997 deficit-to-GDP ratio back to 3.2 percent from 3.8 percent, IFO said.
That level still exceeds the Maastricht Treaty reference value of three percent.
IFO went on to say that it did not expect the Bundesbank to cut its key discount or Lombard rates any further, but said that a slight easing of the securities repurchase rate was possible.
The institute also predicted that the dollar would trade in a range between 1.50 and 1.55 marks in 1997, with a tendency towards the higher end of this range.
IFO also forecast that Germany's current account deficit would fall to 12 billion marks in 1997 from an expected 26 billion marks in 1996.
An expected rise in Germany's trading surplus to 117 billion marks from 95 billion would help narrow the deficit, the institute said.
Earlier, IFO reported a surprising fall in its business climate index for November, interrupting a strong growth trend in recent months.
IFO said the West German index fell to 96.9 from a revised 97.3 in October.
However economists said the slip was likely to be temporary and was probably caused by anxiety over a recent spate of labour unrest.
